Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: Gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#0]. The typical symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation, meaning stomach contents come back up into the throat [18#1]. Several factors can raise a person's risk of developing GERD, including weakness in the esophageal lining's defenses, problems with how the esophagus and stomach move and clear food, and anatomical defects such as a hiatal hernia [19#2]. In children, GERD is less common than simple reflux and is a disease process that causes troublesome symptoms needing careful evaluation and sometimes medical treatment [19#3]. Symptoms that might come from GERD are among the most common reasons people report problems to their primary care doctors [20#4]. Left untreated, GERD can reduce quality of life and lead to serious problems including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and Barrett esophagus, which can develop into esophageal cancer [18#5].

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat or mouth [18#0]. The disease happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#1]. In children, the signs can be varied and hard to pin down, and the condition involves involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus [19#2][19#3]. Symptoms that may be caused by GERD are among the most common complaints people bring to their primary care doctors [20#4]. Risk factors for GERD include abnormal relaxations of the valve between the esophagus and stomach, weaknesses in the esophagus's protective lining, problems with how the esophagus and stomach move and clear contents, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#5][19#6][19#7][19#8]. The condition can lead to serious complications including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and Barrett esophagus, which can precede esophageal cancer [18#9]. Long-term use of the most common treatment, proton-pump inhibitors, carries its own risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#10]. The findings also include several publications and clinical trials related to GERD. PubMed publications include PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17]. Clinical trials listed are Famotidine in Subjects With Non-erosive Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [4], Efficacy of Pantoprazole in Patients Older Than 18 Years Who Have Symptoms of Acid Reflux (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) (BY1023/M3-339) [7], Natural History of Gastroesophageal Reflux (GER) in Children and Adolescents [10], On Demand Treatment of Reflux Disease [13], and Treatment Of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease By Endoscopic Fundoplication, A Placebo-Controlled Study [16]. A MedGen record for Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) is also present [2], along with a literature entity named Gastroesophageal Reflux [3].
